title: Inferring Globular Cluster Initial Mass Function from Stellar Streams
comment: 8 pages, 10 figures, submitted to ApJL. Comments welcome
summary: The Gaia mission has provided precise astrometry and spectrophotometry for billions of stars in the Milky Way, enabling the identification and kinematic characterization of stellar streams. These streams, remnants of disrupted globular clusters and dwarf galaxies, have revealed the structure of the Milky Way's dark matter halo. We show that stellar streams also encode information about the initial mass function of globular clusters. We combine cold dark matter simulations that model the evolution and disruption of embedded globular clusters with observations of stellar streams and globular clusters to infer the initial cluster mass function. We find that initially more massive clusters produce more massive streams, but deposit a smaller fraction of their initial mass into those streams. Using stream mass and angular momentum measurements, we recover a declining, power-law-like initial mass function with a slope $α= 1.3\pm0.05$ for streams $\gtrsim 1000\,M_{\odot}$. This work establishes stellar streams as a novel probe of the early mass distribution of globular clusters.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that stellar streams encode information about the initial mass function of globular clusters. Using simulations and observations, the authors infer a declining power-law initial cluster mass function with slope α = 1.3 ± 0.05 for streams ≳ 1000 M☉, establishing stellar streams as a novel probe of early globular cluster mass distribution.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that stellar streams, beyond revealing dark matter halo structure, also encode information about the initial mass function of globular clusters, providing a new probe of early cluster mass distribution.
AI.method: Combined cold dark matter simulations of the evolution and disruption of embedded globular clusters with observations of stellar streams and globular clusters to infer the initial cluster mass function.
AI.result: More massive clusters produce more massive streams but deposit a smaller fraction of their initial mass into those streams. Using stream mass and angular momentum measurements, a power-law initial mass function with slope α = 1.3 ± 0.05 is recovered for streams ≳ 1000 M☉.
AI.conclusion: Stellar streams serve as a novel probe of the early mass distribution of globular clusters, enabling inference of the initial cluster mass function.

title: On the correlation between globular clusters and the distribution of dark matter in galaxy clusters: the case of Abell 2744
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures - scripts available here: https://github.com/mreinacampos/starclusters-in-jwst/tree/a3df64fa8a821ece9ebc014b7010066971a07958/code_poisson_comparison/abell2744 - submitted to ApJ, comments welcome!
summary: Globular clusters (GCs) lie scattered around the inner $40\%$ of the virial radius of galaxy clusters, potentially being excellent tracers of the underlying mass distribution. In this paper, we present a statistical method based on assuming that the location of GCs around a galaxy cluster follows an inhomogenous spatial Poisson point process, and we use this method to assess to which galactic component GCs are better tracers of. We apply the method to the galaxy cluster Abell 2744, and we find that the spatial distribution of bright GCs roughly traces the three main interacting clumps in the galaxy cluster, alongside other galaxies with sizeable GC populations. The GC populations are more closely correlated to the predicted mass maps than any other galactic component (Spearman rank coefficients $>0.7$). A perk of this statistical method is that it allows us to distinguish to which map the agreement is closest to. In particular, we find that the Bright Blue GCs are compatible with the mass map solely derived from weak lensing, suggesting that they can provide complementary and independent information on the mass distribution in galaxy clusters with a similar level of detail to that of weak lensing. This statistical method is available in a public repository, and combined with catalogs of GCs in galaxy clusters at different cosmic epochs, it provides an independent method for investigating the mass distribution in these galactic environments.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a statistical method based on inhomogenous spatial Poisson point processes to assess how well globular clusters (GCs) trace mass distributions in galaxy clusters. Applied to Abell 2744, bright GCs correlate strongly (Spearman >0.7) with predicted mass maps, with Bright Blue GCs particularly compatible with weak-lensing-derived mass maps, offering independent mass tracers.
AI.motivation: Globular clusters lie within the inner 40% of the virial radius of galaxy clusters and may serve as excellent tracers of underlying mass distribution, but a rigorous statistical framework to quantify this tracing capability was lacking.
AI.method: A statistical method modeling GC locations as an inhomogenous spatial Poisson point process; applied to Abell 2744 to compare GC spatial distributions against predicted mass maps and other galactic components using Spearman rank correlation.
AI.result: Bright GCs roughly trace the three main interacting clumps in Abell 2744; GC populations correlate more closely with predicted mass maps than any other galactic component (Spearman >0.7); Bright Blue GCs are specifically compatible with weak-lensing-derived mass maps.
AI.conclusion: GCs, especially Bright Blue ones, can provide complementary and independent information on mass distribution in galaxy clusters at a level of detail similar to weak lensing. The statistical method is publicly available and applicable across cosmic epochs.

title: Formation of intermediate-mass black holes in young massive clusters detected with JWST: analytic mass estimates
comment: Submitted to A&A
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a population of dense stellar systems at high redshift, including the "Cosmic Gems" arc ($z \sim 10.2$) and the "Firefly Sparkle" ($z \sim 8.3$). With masses in the range of $10^5$~M$_\odot$-$10^7$M$_\odot$ and half-mass radii in the range from $\sim0.4$-$15$ pc, these systems are ideally suited to form intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) via collision-based models. While direct N-body simulations are unfeasible for such a large population and given the high masses in many of the clusters, we estimate the IMBH masses formed via runaway stellar collisions in these specific environments utilizing a Fokker-Planck model together with an analytical framework for runaway collisions and mass loss through winds, which has been validated against direct N-body simulations of compact star clusters. We apply this model to a sample of massive high-redshift clusters observed with JWST. Our estimates yield typical IMBH masses in the range of $\sim10^2$ M$_\odot$ {\bf up to $\sim4\times 10^3$ M$_\odot$,} implying typical formation efficiencies on the few percent level. The extreme compactness of the Cosmic Gems clusters ($R_h \sim 1$ pc) facilitates the formation of black hole seeds with high masses of $1600-2700 {\rm M}_\odot$. Low metallicity ($Z \lesssim 0.02 \, {\rm Z}_\odot$) is a critical factor for retaining the seed mass against stellar winds. We further demonstrate that the efficiencies obtained here are consistent with expectations based on direct N-body simulations. Our results suggest that these dense, metal-poor clusters are viable factories for heavy seeds, capable of growing into the supermassive black holes observed in the early Universe.

AI.tldr: JWST-discovered dense stellar systems at high redshift (z~8-10) are studied for their potential to form intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) via runaway stellar collisions. Using a Fokker-Planck model and analytical framework validated against N-body simulations, the authors estimate IMBH masses of ~10²–4×10³ M☉ with formation efficiencies of a few percent. The Cosmic Gems arc (Rh~1 pc) can produce black hole seeds of 1600–2700 M☉. Low metallicity (Z≲0.02 Z☉) is crucial for seed mass retention. These clusters are viable factories for heavy seeds that could grow into supermassive black holes in the early Universe.
AI.motivation: JWST has discovered compact, high-redshift stellar clusters (e.g., Cosmic Gems at z~10.2, Firefly Sparkle at z~8.3) with masses 10⁵–10⁷ M☉ and half-mass radii 0.4–15 pc, which are ideal environments for forming IMBHs via collision-based models. The authors aim to assess whether these observed systems can produce heavy black hole seeds.
AI.method: The authors use a Fokker-Planck model combined with an analytical framework for runaway collisions and stellar wind mass loss, validated against direct N-body simulations of compact star clusters, to estimate IMBH masses formed in JWST-observed high-redshift clusters.
AI.result: Estimated IMBH masses range from ~10² M☉ up to ~4×10³ M☉, with formation efficiencies at a few percent level. The Cosmic Gems arc, with extreme compactness (Rh~1 pc), yields black hole seeds of 1600–2700 M☉. Low metallicity (Z≲0.02 Z☉) is critical for retaining seed mass. Derived efficiencies are consistent with direct N-body simulation expectations.
AI.conclusion: Dense, metal-poor high-redshift clusters are viable factories for heavy black hole seeds capable of growing into the supermassive black holes observed in the early Universe.

title: Simulation-Based Prediction of Black Hole Fe K$α$ Line Profiles
comment: Accepted to ApJ
summary: One of the most useful spectral diagnostics of accreting black hole systems is the Fe K$α$ fluorescence line. Detected in many systems, it is often used to estimate the black hole spin, as its breadth is attributed to relativistic kinematics near the spin-dependent innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO). In a companion paper, we showed how continuum spectra emitted by accreting black holes can be derived from snapshots of general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics simulations by combining radiation transfer solutions for the disk body and the corona. In this paper, we focus on the Fe K$α$ line, solving its transfer problem on the basis of local ionization and thermal balance. Its equivalent width is $\sim 25-225$ eV, depending mainly on viewing angle, for an accretion rate of 1$\%$ Eddington. Contrary to common assumptions, the illuminating X-ray spectrum and ionization parameter $ξ$ can be strong functions of radius; e.g. $ξ\propto r^{-1.5}$ in this simulation. Consequently, the region of the disk near the ISCO is completely ionized and contributes almost no Fe K$α$ photons; most of the flux is made at radii $\gtrsim 10 r_g$. The lines are broadened by a combination of relativistic Doppler shifts, Compton broadening in the disk atmosphere, and the differing line energies emitted by different Fe ions. These new mechanisms expand the parameter space of acceptable models, including the possibility of broad line profiles without large black hole spin; physical trends revealed by the simulations can refocus fitting efforts on the most relevant sections of the parameter space.

AI.tldr: This paper presents radiation transfer simulations of the Fe Kα line from accreting black holes, showing that the line's equivalent width (25-225 eV) depends mainly on viewing angle, the inner disk near ISCO is fully ionized and contributes little Fe Kα flux (most comes from radii ≳ 10 r_g), and broadening arises from relativistic effects, Compton scattering, and multiple Fe ionization states, which can produce broad line profiles without requiring high black hole spin.
AI.motivation: To model the Fe Kα fluorescence line from accreting black holes using physically self-consistent radiation transfer solutions based on GRMHD simulations and local ionization/thermal balance, rather than relying on simplified assumptions about the illuminating spectrum and ionization parameter.
AI.method: Radiation transfer calculations for the Fe Kα line are performed on snapshots from general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations, solving for local ionization and thermal balance to determine the line production and transport.
AI.result: Equivalent width ranges from ~25-225 eV depending on viewing angle at 1% Eddington accretion rate. The ionization parameter ξ ∝ r^{-1.5}, causing the inner disk near ISCO to be fully ionized. Most Fe Kα flux originates at radii ≳ 10 r_g. Line broadening results from relativistic Doppler shifts, Compton broadening, and multiple Fe ion line energies.
AI.conclusion: Broad Fe Kα line profiles can occur without requiring large black hole spin, expanding the viable parameter space for spectral fitting and redirecting attention to physically motivated regions of parameter space.

title: Milky Way Mapper decoded abundances -- I. Shared disc enrichment patterns
comment: accepted MNRAS
summary: Elemental abundances in the Milky Way disc trace its star-formation and enrichment history, but predicting these abundances from theory is limited by uncertain nucleosynthetic yields and poorly constrained chemical evolution models. Large surveys provide many abundances that enable multi-dimensional insight. However, having so much data available complicates joint visualisation and physical interpretation. Here, we examine the element abundances of 70,057 red giant stars from the Milky Way Mapper survey ([Fe/H] $> -1$), using 16 elements (O,~Mg,~Al,~Si,~S,~K,~Ca,~Ti,~V, ~Cr, Mn,~Fe,~Co,~Ni,~Ce,~Nd). To tackle the challenges of joint-interpretation of these elements, we build a generative data-driven model, expressing each star's abundance vector as a linear combination of a few ($4$) latent nucleosynthetic patterns. These patterns are shared among the population but vary in fraction between stars. The model accurately generates the measured abundances, with $χ^2 < 3$ (5) for $\sim$ 80\% (95\%) of stars. Model failures, where stars' abundances are not generated by the latent basis reveal accreted material and the role of multiple channels of metal-poor disk enrichment. We associate the recovered patterns, which represent high-precision ($σ_P \sim 3$\%) nucleosynthetic channels, with specific enrichment sources; (early and late) core-collapse supernovae, supernovae Type Ia, and asymptotic giant branch stars. We subsequently explore how the dominance of enrichment channels varies across age, metallicity and spatial extent of the disk, and show that enrichment patterns tightly couple to orbital properties. Mean pattern fractions vary smoothly with enrichment, and change rapidly across the valley between the high- and low-$α$ sequences. Our results provide a framework for improving our understanding of Galactic evolution in the Milky Way.

AI.tldr: A generative data-driven model using 4 latent nucleosynthetic patterns accurately reconstructs abundance measurements for 70,057 red giants from the Milky Way Mapper survey, linking patterns to enrichment sources (CCSNe, SNe Ia, AGB stars) and revealing how enrichment channels vary with age, metallicity, and orbital properties across the Galactic disk.
AI.motivation: To overcome the challenges of jointly interpreting multi-element abundance data from large spectroscopic surveys, enabling physical insight into Galactic chemical evolution despite uncertain nucleosynthetic yields and complex enrichment histories.
AI.method: Built a generative data-driven model that expresses each star's abundance vector as a linear combination of 4 shared latent nucleosynthetic patterns. The model was applied to 70,057 red giants from the Milky Way Mapper survey, using 16 elements with [Fe/H] > -1.
AI.result: Model achieves χ² < 3 for ~80% of stars and χ² < 5 for ~95% of stars. Model failures identify accreted material and multiple channels of metal-poor disk enrichment. The 4 latent patterns correspond to early/late core-collapse SNe, SNe Type Ia, and AGB stars with ~3% precision. Pattern fractions vary smoothly with enrichment, metallicity, age, and orbital properties, and change rapidly across the high-/low-α sequence valley.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully separates and quantifies nucleosynthetic channels from observational data, providing a new approach to improve understanding of Galactic chemical evolution in the Milky Way.

title: Guide-Field-mediated Multiscale Instabilities in Relativistic Reconnection
summary: We investigate magnetic-energy dissipation, current-sheet dynamics, and nonthermal particle acceleration in three-dimensional relativistic reconnection in an electron--ion plasma with a realistic mass ratio. Using particle-in-cell simulations of a double Harris current sheet, we explore a range of ion magnetisations and guide-field strengths to determine how guide fields regulate the overall magnetic energy dissipation. At low magnetisation, $σ_i=0.1$, increasing the guide field suppresses reconnection: magnetic-energy dissipation decreases, the growth of tearing modes is weakened, and nonthermal particle acceleration remains inefficient. At higher magnetisations, $σ_i=1$ and $σ_i=5$, the behaviour changes qualitatively. In the zero-guide-field case, strong drift-kink activity corrugates and broadens the current sheet, inhibiting efficient tearing-mediated reconnection. A weak guide field suppresses this drift-kink-driven disruption, allowing the current sheet to remain laminar and more coherent and thereby enhancing magnetic-energy dissipation. However, once the guide field becomes too strong, reconnection is again suppressed: the onset is delayed, tearing activity weakens, current-sheet compression is reduced, and the system retains a larger fraction of its initial magnetic energy. This non-monotonic behaviour is reflected consistently in magnetic-energy evolution, Fourier analysis of the tearing and kink modes, current-sheet thickness, and nonthermal particle acceleration. The most dissipative cases are not necessarily the zero-guide-field runs, but rather those in which the guide field balances drift-kink suppression without strongly impeding the tearing modes. Our results show that the overall system evolution is controlled not only by the available magnetic energy, but also by the guide-field-regulated morphology and stability of the reconnecting current sheet.

AI.tldr: This study uses 3D PIC simulations of relativistic reconnection in electron-ion plasmas with realistic mass ratios to show that the guide field non-monotonically regulates magnetic energy dissipation, current-sheet dynamics, and nonthermal particle acceleration, with optimal dissipation occurring when the guide field suppresses disruptive drift-kink instabilities without overly impeding tearing modes.
AI.motivation: To understand how guide fields regulate magnetic energy dissipation, current-sheet morphology, and nonthermal particle acceleration in 3D relativistic reconnection in electron-ion plasmas with a realistic mass ratio, across a range of ion magnetizations.
AI.method: 3D particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations of a double Harris current sheet in an electron-ion plasma with realistic mass ratio, varying ion magnetization (σ_i = 0.1, 1, 5) and guide-field strength.
AI.result: At low magnetization (σ_i=0.1), increasing guide field suppresses reconnection. At higher magnetizations (σ_i=1,5), a weak guide field enhances dissipation by suppressing drift-kink disruption, but a strong guide field again suppresses reconnection. The most dissipative cases balance drift-kink suppression without impeding tearing modes.
AI.conclusion: System evolution is controlled not only by available magnetic energy but also by guide-field-regulated current-sheet morphology and stability; optimal dissipation occurs at intermediate guide-field strengths.

title: Dynamical Cluster Assembly Framework (D-CAF): The Link Between Star Cluster Formation and Expansion Rates
comment: 25 pages, 10 figures. Submitted to Apj
summary: We introduce the Dynamical Cluster Assembly Framework (D-CAF), an AMUSE-based framework designed to connect embedded star formation histories to the dynamical evolution of young stellar systems. We model star formation through the gradual formation of stars inside an evolving background potential, where the global gas evolution is extracted from realistic magneto-hydrodynamical (MHD) simulations. In this first work, we focus on the global evolution of the natal gas and its dynamical imprint on the stellar population. Across all explored MHD setups, we find that the gas continues to collapse while stars are forming, increasing both the central concentration and velocity scale of the embedded stellar population before gas expulsion. Using a controlled grid of direct $N$-body simulations, we show that this embedded evolution strongly regulates both the survival and later expansion of young stellar systems. In particular, gas contraction shortens the stellar crossing time prior to gas expulsion, making the same gas-removal timescale effectively more adiabatic for the stars. We find that the present-day expansion of stellar associations still preserves information about the embedded dynamical state reached during formation. The expansion rate is limited by the velocity scale reached before gas expulsion, while the efficiency with which this velocity field is transformed into expansion depends on the gas-expulsion timescale. Finally, we show that some commonly used expansion diagnostics can directly trace the physical expansion rate of young stellar systems when full kinematic information is available, opening the possibility of using stellar kinematics to constrain the dynamical conditions of embedded star formation.

AI.tldr: D-CAF connects embedded star formation to the dynamical evolution of young stellar systems, finding that gas contraction during star formation regulates stellar system survival and expansion, with expansion diagnostics preserving information about the embedded dynamical state.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between realistic star formation histories from MHD simulations and the dynamical evolution of young stellar systems, understanding how natal gas evolution imprints on stellar populations.
AI.method: The Dynamical Cluster Assembly Framework (D-CAF) uses AMUSE to model gradual star formation inside an evolving background potential extracted from MHD simulations, combined with direct N-body simulations across a controlled grid of setups.
AI.result: Gas continues to collapse during star formation, increasing central concentration and velocity scale of the embedded population. Gas contraction shortens the stellar crossing time before gas expulsion, making gas removal more adiabatic. Present-day expansion preserves information about the embedded dynamical state.
AI.conclusion: Expansion diagnostics can trace physical expansion rates when full kinematics are available, enabling the use of stellar kinematics to constrain the dynamical conditions of embedded star formation.

title: On the origin of anomalous dissipation in simulations of tidal disruption events
comment: 22 pages, 13 figures, 1 appendix, submitted
summary: In a tidal disruption event (TDE), a star is destroyed by the tidal field of a supermassive black hole. The stellar debris is initially placed on highly elliptical orbits, and a longstanding question in TDE theory is: How does the stellar debris circularize into a disc and accrete? The originally proposed answer to this question is self-intersection shocks, where relativistic apsidal precession results in a strong collision between the incoming and outgoing material. However, global simulations of TDEs tend to find enhanced hydrodynamical dissipation prior to any intersections of the debris orbits, with the material ``fanning out'' into a wide-angle and partially-unbound outflow upon passing through pericenter. We show that this dissipation is numerical in origin and arises from a combination of 1) the change in the kinematics of the debris as it passes through pericenter, with its velocity profile along the stream transitioning from strongly diverging pre-pericenter to strongly converging post-pericenter, and 2) the dependence of numerical algorithms (viscosity switches for particle-based methods and Riemann solvers for Godunov-based schemes) on the diverging vs. converging nature of the fluid. We support this conclusion with analytical and numerical modeling. We discuss possible resolutions to these issues as well as the implications of our findings in the context of observations.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that the enhanced hydrodynamical dissipation observed in TDE simulations before debris orbit intersections is not physical but numerical, arising from how numerical algorithms handle the transition from diverging to converging flow at pericenter.
AI.motivation: A longstanding question in TDE theory is how stellar debris circularizes into a disc and accretes. While self-intersection shocks from relativistic precession were originally proposed, simulations show enhanced dissipation before any debris orbit intersections occur, with material "fanning out" into a wide-angle outflow. The cause of this pre-intersection dissipation was unclear.
AI.method: The authors combine analytical modeling and numerical simulations to investigate the origin of enhanced dissipation in TDEs. They analyze the kinematics of debris stream as it passes through pericenter, noting the velocity profile transitions from strongly diverging pre-pericenter to strongly converging post-pericenter. They then examine how different numerical algorithms (viscosity switches for particle-based methods and Riemann solvers for Godunov-based schemes) respond to this transition.
AI.result: The enhanced dissipation is numerical in origin, caused by two factors: (1) the natural kinematic transition of the debris stream from diverging to converging flow at pericenter, and (2) the dependence of numerical algorithms on whether the fluid is diverging or converging. This numerical artifact mimics physical dissipation and leads to the "fanning out" seen in simulations.
AI.conclusion: The widespread numerical dissipation in TDE simulations is artificial. The authors discuss potential resolutions to these numerical issues and explore the implications of their findings for interpreting observational data of TDEs.

title: The chemo-dynamical complexity of ω Centauri: different kinematics for different populations
comment: Submitted to A&A
summary: The origin of ω Centauri remains one of the key open problems in stellar dynamics and chemical evolution. Its large abundance spreads and multiple populations suggest a formation history more complex than that of a typical globular cluster. We investigate whether the chemical sub-populations identified in APOGEE DR17 also exhibit distinct spatial and kinematic signatures. We analyse a sample of APOGEE DR17 red-giant stars using a Gaussian Mixture Model in an eight-dimensional chemical-abundance space. The resulting chemical components are combined with Gaia proper motions and APOGEE line-of-sight velocities to derive intrinsic mean velocities and velocity dispersions in all three observable directions. We measure both global kinematic quantities and radial profiles for each chemically defined group, extending from the inner regions to ~ 4 half-light radii. The Gaussian Mixture Model identifies five chemical components, which, when examined through their radial cumulative distributions, naturally group into two broader families characterised by lower and higher aluminium enrichment. The two families differ significantly in their spatial and kinematic properties: the Al-rich stars are more centrally concentrated and exhibit stronger radial anisotropy than the Al-poor stars, which remain closer to isotropy over the radial range probed. Despite these significant differences, the two populations share a common rotation pattern. This work represents the first chemo-dynamical study of ω Cen linking detailed chemical tagging to internal kinematics from the inner regions to the cluster outskirts. A formation path involving both hierarchical assembly within a dwarf-galaxy potential and centrally concentrated, chemically enriched star formation offers a natural explanation for the observed chemo-dynamical complexity.

AI.tldr: This study investigates the chemo-dynamical properties of ω Centauri using APOGEE DR17 and Gaia data. A Gaussian Mixture Model in 8D chemical-abundance space identifies five chemical components grouped into Al-poor and Al-rich families. Al-rich stars are more centrally concentrated and radially anisotropic, while both populations share a common rotation pattern. Results support a formation scenario involving hierarchical assembly within a dwarf galaxy plus centrally concentrated enriched star formation.
AI.motivation: The origin of ω Centauri remains a key open problem in stellar dynamics and chemical evolution due to its large chemical abundance spreads and multiple populations, suggesting a more complex formation history than typical globular clusters.
AI.method: APOGEE DR17 red-giant stars are analyzed using a Gaussian Mixture Model in eight-dimensional chemical-abundance space. Identified chemical components are combined with Gaia proper motions and APOGEE line-of-sight velocities to derive intrinsic mean velocities and velocity dispersions. Radial profiles extending to ~4 half-light radii are measured for each chemically defined group.
AI.result: Five chemical components are identified, grouping into Al-poor and Al-rich families. Al-rich stars are more centrally concentrated and exhibit stronger radial anisotropy, while Al-poor stars remain closer to isotropy. Both populations share a common rotation pattern despite significant spatial and kinematic differences.
AI.conclusion: The observed chemo-dynamical complexity is naturally explained by a formation path involving both hierarchical assembly within a dwarf-galaxy potential and centrally concentrated, chemically enriched star formation.

title: Spider-Webb: enhanced star formation in low-mass galaxies within the Spiderweb protocluster revealed by JWST Pa$β$ narrow-band imaging
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Understanding the role of the environment in galaxy evolution is key to revealing the physical processes that regulate galaxy growth. We study the star formation activity of \pab\ emitters (PBEs) in the Spiderweb protocluster at $z=2.16$ using \textit{James Webb Space Telescope}/NIRCam narrow-band imaging. To investigate the environmental dependence of star formation, we derive star formation rates (SFRs) from the \pab\ emission line and compare SFRs in the Spiderweb protocluster with those in the field. Our main finding is that low-mass PBEs ($M_\star < 10^9\,M_\odot$) in the Spiderweb protocluster exhibit an enhancement in star formation compared to their field counterparts. This excess persists even without applying dust-attenuation corrections, indicating that enhanced star formation in the protocluster is robust regardless of whether a dust correction is applied. In contrast, intermediate- and high-mass PBEs ($M_\star > 10^9\,M_\odot$) show no significant deviation from the field, revealing a strong mass dependence in the environmental effects on star formation. No clear spatial concentration toward the cluster core of starbursting low-mass galaxies within the protocluster is seen, suggesting that their enhancement is not restricted to the cluster core. We suggest that starbursts in low-mass galaxies are facilitated by environmental processes such as galaxy mergers/interactions, and/or efficient gas supply. While the enhancement at the low-mass end is consistent with trends reported for other protoclusters at similar redshifts, the behaviour of star formation at intermediate masses ($10^{9} < M_\star/M_\odot < 10^{10}$) is not uniform across protoclusters. Our \pab-based results in the Spiderweb protocluster indicate that star-formation enhancement at cosmic noon depends on both mass and the dynamical state of the protocluster.

AI.tldr: This paper studies star formation in the Spiderweb protocluster at z=2.16 using JWST narrow-band imaging of Paα emitters (PBEs). Low-mass galaxies (M★ < 10^9 M☉) show enhanced star formation compared to field galaxies, while higher-mass galaxies show no significant difference. This enhancement is robust regardless of dust correction and not spatially concentrated to the cluster core, suggesting environmental processes like mergers or gas supply drive starbursts in low-mass galaxies.
AI.motivation: To understand how environment regulates galaxy growth by investigating the environmental dependence of star formation activity at z=2.16, using the Spiderweb protocluster as a case study to reveal physical processes that modulate star formation in dense environments during cosmic noon.
AI.method: JWST/NIRCam narrow-band imaging of Paα emitters (PBEs) in the Spiderweb protocluster at z=2.16; derivation of SFRs from Paα emission line; comparison of SFRs between protocluster and field; analysis of mass dependence and spatial distribution.
AI.result: Low-mass PBEs (M★ < 10^9 M☉) in the Spiderweb protocluster show enhanced star formation compared to field counterparts, robust to dust-attenuation corrections. Intermediate- and high-mass PBEs (M★ > 10^9 M☉) show no significant deviation. No clear spatial concentration of low-mass starbursting galaxies toward the cluster core.
AI.conclusion: Starbursts in low-mass galaxies in the protocluster are likely driven by environmental processes such as mergers/interactions or efficient gas supply. Star-formation enhancement at cosmic noon depends on both galaxy mass and the dynamical state of the protocluster. The low-mass enhancement is consistent with other protoclusters, but intermediate-mass behavior is not uniform across different protoclusters.

title: Binary Neutron Star Merger Evolution and r-Process Enrichment in the Milky Way Disk
comment: Comments are welcome!
summary: The origin of half of the rapid neutron-capture nucleosynthesis (r-process) elements in the Universe remains an open question. Binary neutron star (BNS) mergers have been shown to face difficulties in reproducing the observed r-process enrichment in Milky Way disk stars. However, their r-process enrichment efficiency may evolve with redshift beyond the star formation history, potentially due to evolution in the merger rate or the average r-process yield in the early Universe. In this paper, we explore the possibility that BNS mergers with an evolving enrichment efficiency could serve as the sole r-process production channel. By jointly comparing gravitational-wave observations from LIGO--Virgo--KAGRA, short gamma-ray bursts, Galactic neutron star populations, and stellar abundance measurements in Milky Way disk stars, we find that scenarios with additional evolution are strongly preferred over non-evolving scenarios, with Bayes factors exceeding $10^{20}$. We quantify the required evolution in both the merger rate and yield, and directly compare them with observations and theoretical predictions. We find that the evolved scenarios are in tension with short gamma-ray burst observations and predictions from multiple population synthesis models, while remaining consistent with current stochastic gravitational-wave background constraints. Our results provide a quantitative framework for evaluating whether BNS mergers with evolving enrichment efficiency can account for the observed r-process enrichment history of Milky Way disk stars.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether binary neutron star (BNS) mergers with evolving enrichment efficiency (varying merger rate or r-process yield) can be the sole source of r-process elements, finding that evolved scenarios are strongly preferred statistically but face tensions with short gamma-ray burst observations and population synthesis models.
AI.motivation: Half of r-process elements in the Universe have an unknown origin; BNS mergers face difficulties explaining observed r-process enrichment in Milky Way disk stars under standard assumptions.
AI.method: Joint Bayesian analysis comparing gravitational-wave (LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA), short gamma-ray bursts, Galactic neutron star populations, and stellar abundance data; Bayes factor comparison between non-evolving and evolving enrichment efficiency scenarios.
AI.result: Evolving scenarios are strongly preferred (Bayes factors >10^20); evolved scenarios tension with SGRB observations and population synthesis models, but consistent with stochastic gravitational-wave background constraints.
AI.conclusion: BNS mergers with evolving enrichment efficiency face observational tensions, providing a quantitative framework to evaluate their viability as the sole r-process channel.

title: Connecting CGM enrichment with Lyman alpha emitters at 2.9 < z < 6.7
comment: 24 pages, 15 figures, Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: We present the results of a blind search for Lyman $α$ emitters (LAEs) in three deep archival $z\sim6$ quasar fields from VLT/MUSE using state-of-the-art detection algorithms. We explore their connection with absorbers-particularly C IV and Mg II-in the circumgalactic medium (CGM) from the E-XQR-30 survey. We detect 156 LAEs at $2.9<z<6.7$ with luminosities ranging from log $L[\text{ergs}^{-1}]=$ 41.3 to 43.2. We find 34 and 14 galaxy associations with C IV and Mg II absorption respectively at $3.4<z<5.8$ within a line of sight velocity window of $\pm1000~\text{km}^{-1}$ and impact parameter of $<250$ pkpc. These systems have a weak anti-correlation with respect to the absorber strength-impact parameter relation. No Mg II systems are found within the virial radii of any LAE while four C IV absorbers are located within the virial radii of an LAE suggesting that low ionisation gas has a lower covering fraction. The LAEs have mild overdensity ratios of 1.7 and 1.9 around C IV and Mg II respectively. The stellar mass upper limits of $\text{log}~M_*<10.7~\text{M}_\odot$ estimated using Keck/NIRC2 imaging indicate that a low-mass, faint population of galaxies pollutes the CGM with metals. This paper serves as a pilot analysis for the forthcoming REQUIEM survey, an ESO Large Program on high redshift deep quasar fields.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a blind search for Lyman α emitters (LAEs) in three deep z~6 quasar fields from VLT/MUSE, detecting 156 LAEs at 2.9<z<6.7. They find 34 and 14 galaxy associations with C IV and Mg II absorption in the CGM respectively, revealing weak anti-correlations with absorber strength-impact parameter relations, no Mg II within virial radii of LAEs, and low covering fraction for low-ionization gas. Stellar mass upper limits suggest low-mass faint galaxies pollute the CGM with metals. This is a pilot for the REQUIEM survey.
AI.motivation: To explore the connection between Lyman α emitters and metal absorbers (C IV and Mg II) in the circumgalactic medium at high redshift (z~6), and to understand how low-mass galaxies enrich the CGM with metals.
AI.method: Blind search for LAEs in three deep archival z~6 quasar fields using VLT/MUSE with state-of-the-art detection algorithms. Cross-matched with C IV and Mg II absorbers from the E-XQR-30 survey within ±1000 km/s velocity window and <250 pkpc impact parameter. Stellar mass upper limits estimated using Keck/NIRC2 imaging.
AI.result: Detected 156 LAEs (2.9<z<6.7, log L=41.3-43.2 erg/s). Found 34 C IV and 14 Mg II galaxy associations. Weak anti-correlation between absorber strength and impact parameter. No Mg II absorbers within LAE virial radii; four C IV absorbers within virial radii. LAE overdensity ratios of 1.7 (C IV) and 1.9 (Mg II). Stellar mass upper limits log M*<10.7 M⊙.
AI.conclusion: Low-ionization gas (Mg II) has lower covering fraction around LAEs. A low-mass, faint galaxy population pollutes the CGM with metals at high redshift. This pilot analysis sets the stage for the forthcoming REQUIEM survey.

title: Multi-wavelength Emission for a Post-merger Magnetar: The Magnetar-Driven Poynting Jet and Its Associated Pulsar Wind Nebula
comment: Accepted by ApJ
summary: A newborn, rapidly rotating magnetar may form in a binary neutron star merger and drive a Poynting-flux-dominated relativistic jet. As the jet propagates outward, a forward shock (FS) and a reverse shock (RS) are formed, inflating a pulsar wind nebula (PWN) between them. We present a systematic study of the emission from both the PWN and the jet, whose magnetic energy is subject to dissipation. By following the dynamics of the jet-ejecta-PWN system, we find that, in most cases, the RS is long-lived: it first lags behind the contact discontinuity and eventually coincides with both the contact discontinuity and the FS after the jet breakout into the external medium. As a result, the emission exhibits a characteristic temporal evolution. Depending on the optical depth, the emission is initially dominated by thermal radiation from the optically thick ejecta, then by a jet-powered X-ray plateau once the system becomes optically thin, and finally by synchrotron and inverse-Compton radiation from the PWN FS at late times. In particular, external inverse-Compton scattering of jet photons by the FS naturally produces a late-time GeV bump together with a substantial TeV component. Our model can simultaneously account for early thermal emission, X-ray plateaus, and late-time GeV excesses in merger-driven gamma-ray bursts, and also indicates that post-merger magnetar-driven PWNs are potential TeV photon sources.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the emission from a magnetar-driven pulsar wind nebula (PWN) formed after a binary neutron star merger, finding that the reverse shock is long-lived, and the emission evolves from thermal to X-ray plateau to synchrotron/IC radiation, explaining early thermal emission, X-ray plateaus, and GeV/TeV excesses in gamma-ray bursts.
AI.motivation: To systematically study the emission from both the PWN and the relativistic jet in post-merger systems with a newborn magnetar, particularly focusing on magnetic energy dissipation, and to understand the multi-wavelength observational signatures.
AI.method: The authors follow the dynamics of the jet-ejecta-PWN system, considering forward shock (FS) and reverse shock (RS) formation, and compute emission components including thermal radiation, synchrotron, and inverse-Compton (IC) scattering, accounting for optical depth evolution.
AI.result: The RS is long-lived, initially lagging behind the contact discontinuity and later coinciding with both the contact discontinuity and the FS after jet breakout. The emission shows a characteristic evolution: thermal-dominated (optically thick), then X-ray plateau (optically thin jet-powered), then synchrotron and IC from the PWN FS. External IC of jet photons by the FS yields a late-time GeV bump and TeV component.
AI.conclusion: The model simultaneously explains early thermal emission, X-ray plateaus, and late-time GeV excesses in merger-driven GRBs. Post-merger magnetar-driven PWNs are potential TeV photon sources.

title: A systematic study of CO/SiO absorption features in early-type galaxies using AKARI/IRC near-infrared spectra
comment: 9 pages, 9 figures, accepted for publication in PASJ
summary: The origin of dust in early-type galaxies (ETGs) remains a long-standing question, with proposed sources being mass loss from evolved stars, galaxy mergers, or grain growth in the interstellar medium. To investigate the dominant source of dust in ETGs, we analyzed near-infrared spectra of 30 ETGs obtained with AKARI, focusing on the SiO and CO absorption features tracing the photospheres of old stellar populations. We also derived the dust mass using near- to far-infrared photometric data obtained by 2MASS, WISE, and AKARI. We find that the dust mass correlates with the summed equivalent widths of the SiO and CO absorption features. This trend suggests that a significant fraction of dust in ETGs may originate from mass loss from evolved stars, consistent with an internal production scenario. The dust mass shows no anti-correlation with diffuse X-ray luminosities, suggesting that dust in ETGs is not strongly interacting with X-ray plasma. Moreover, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are detected in the near-infrared spectra. We find that the PAH intensity shows no correlation with the equivalent widths of SiO and CO, but correlates with the luminosity of hot and warm dust components. This suggests that PAHs may be of external origin associated with galaxy merger remnants, heated by the activities of galactic nuclei.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes AKARI near-infrared spectra and multi-band photometry of 30 early-type galaxies to investigate dust origins. Results show dust mass correlates with SiO/CO absorption strengths (indicating evolved star mass loss) and PAH emission correlates with hot/warm dust luminosity rather than stellar features, suggesting dust has both internal (evolved stars) and external (merger-related) origins.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing question of whether dust in early-type galaxies originates from evolved star mass loss, galaxy mergers, or interstellar grain growth.
AI.method: Near-infrared spectra of 30 ETGs from AKARI were analyzed for SiO and CO absorption features tracing old stellar populations. Dust masses were derived from 2MASS, WISE, and AKARI photometry, and relationships between dust properties, stellar absorption features, X-ray emission, and PAH emission were examined.
AI.result: Dust mass correlates with SiO+CO equivalent widths, supporting internal production from evolved stars. No anti-correlation with diffuse X-ray luminosity indicates weak dust-plasma interaction. PAH intensity does not correlate with SiO/CO but correlates with hot/warm dust luminosity, suggesting external (merger) origin heated by nuclear activity.
AI.conclusion: Dust in ETGs likely has dual origins: a significant fraction is internally produced via mass loss from evolved stars, while PAHs appear to be externally sourced from galaxy mergers and heated by active galactic nuclei.

title: A MINOT-based Study of Gamma-ray emission from SPT-CL J2012-5649/Abell 3667
comment: 22 pages, 13 Figures
summary: We present an analysis of the non-thermal properties of the merging galaxy cluster SPT-CL J2012-5649/Abell~3667 ($z = 0.0556$, $M_{500} = 7.16 \times 10^{14}\ M_\odot$) using the MINOT non-thermal emission modelling framework. The predicted hadronic gamma-ray flux from $pp$ interactions in the $1$--$300\ \mathrm{GeV}$ band is $2.82 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\ s^{-1}}$ within $R_{500}$, rising to $1.15 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\ s^{-1}}$ at the truncation radius ($3.7\,R_{500}$), in order-of-magnitude agreement with the Fermi-LAT reported flux of $1.3 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}\ s^{-1}}$. Approximately $76\%$ of the predicted hadronic flux originates from beyond $R_{500}$. The IC contribution from cosmic-ray electrons is subdominant relative to the hadronic $π^0$-decay gamma-ray component by a factor of ${\sim}20$ in the $1$--$300\ \mathrm{GeV}$ energy band, and therefore does not contribute significantly to the observable signal. Although the expected hadronic flux is in approximate agreement with the observed Fermi-LAT flux level in the $1$--$300\ \mathrm{GeV}$ band, the observed spectral index ($Γ= -3.61 \pm 0.33$) is in tension with the hadronic prediction ($Γ\approx -2.4$ to $-2.6$).

AI.tldr: This paper models non-thermal emission from merging galaxy cluster SPT-CL J2012-5649/Abell 3667 using the MINOT framework, finding hadronic gamma-ray flux from pp interactions agrees within order-of-magnitude with Fermi-LAT observations, but the observed spectral index differs significantly from predictions.
AI.motivation: To understand the non-thermal properties and gamma-ray emission mechanisms of the merging galaxy cluster SPT-CL J2012-5649/Abell 3667 by comparing hadronic and leptonic models with Fermi-LAT observations.
AI.method: Used the MINOT non-thermal emission modelling framework to compute hadronic (pp-induced π⁰-decay) and IC (cosmic-ray electron) gamma-ray emission across 1–300 GeV, comparing predictions with Fermi-LAT data within R₅₀₀ and up to the truncation radius (3.7 R₅₀₀).
AI.result: Predicted hadronic flux: 2.82×10⁻¹¹ cm⁻² s⁻¹ within R₅₀₀, rising to 1.15×10⁻¹⁰ cm⁻² s⁻¹ at truncation radius (order-of-magnitude agreement with Fermi-LAT 1.3×10⁻¹⁰ cm⁻² s⁻¹). 76% of hadronic flux originates beyond R₅₀₀. IC component is subdominant by factor ~20. Spectral index tension: observed Γ=−3.61±0.33 vs. predicted Γ≈−2.4 to −2.6.
AI.conclusion: While the flux level of hadronic gamma-ray emission agrees roughly with Fermi-LAT observations, the significant spectral index mismatch suggests that additional emission mechanisms or physical processes (beyond pure hadronic models) are needed to explain the observed gamma-ray signal from this merging cluster.

title: Characterizing the origins of gamma-ray variability of the jetted active galactic nuclei observed with the Fermi-LAT
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures, accept for publication in the Astrophysical Journal Supplement
summary: We conducted an analysis of gamma-ray variability in a large sample of jetted active galactic nuclei (AGNs) by utilizing archival Fermi-LAT light curves and applying damped random walk modeling to obtain variability amplitude. Our primary findings are summarized as follows: (1) The mean variability damping timescales of our sources are approximately 100 days. This damping timescale may imply that the diffusive shock acceleration plays an important role in the variability of gamma-ray emission. (2) Flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs) demonstrate greater variability amplitude compared to BL Lacertae objects (BL Lacs). (3) The ratio of the distance of the emission region from the central supermassive black hole to the dusty torus radius for our sources is $R\approx2-4.5R_{\rm DT}$. In contrast, the ratio of the distance of the emission region from the central supermassive black hole to the BLR radius for our sources is $R\approx135-295R_{\rm BLR-in}$ and $R\approx123-270R_{\rm BLR-out}$. These findings indicate that the $γ$-ray emission region in jetted AGNs is likely located beyond the BLR, potentially could be associated with the dusty torus. (4) A statistical correlation is observed between variability amplitude and radio luminosity, radio loudness, X-ray luminosity, X-ray loudness, gamma-ray luminosity, and gamma-ray loudness, indicating a potential relationship between gamma-ray variability and jet activity. (5) Variability amplitude also shows a statistical correlations with synchrotron peak frequency luminosity, inverse Compton peak frequency luminosity, and Compton dominance. (6) Variability amplitude also correlates with black hole mass, accretion disk luminosity, and Eddington ratio, implying that the accretion disk may also contribute to gamma-ray variability.

AI.tldr: Analysis of gamma-ray variability in a large sample of jetted AGNs using Fermi-LAT light curves and damped random walk modeling; key findings include ~100-day damping timescales, greater variability in FSRQs than BL Lacs, emission region likely beyond BLR near the dusty torus, and correlations between variability amplitude and jet/accretion-related parameters.
AI.motivation: To understand the physical origins and location of gamma-ray variability in jetted AGNs by systematically characterizing variability amplitudes and damping timescales across a large sample.
AI.method: Utilized archival Fermi-LAT light curves and applied damped random walk (DRW) modeling to derive variability amplitudes and damping timescales for a large sample of jetted AGNs.
AI.result: (1) Mean damping timescale ~100 days, implicating diffusive shock acceleration. (2) FSRQs show larger variability amplitude than BL Lacs. (3) Emission region distance R ~ 2-4.5 R_DT (dusty torus) and R ~ 135-295 R_BLR-in, ~123-270 R_BLR-out, suggesting location beyond BLR near dusty torus. (4)-(6) Variability amplitude correlates with radio/X-ray/gamma-ray luminosities and loudness, synchrotron/IC peak luminosities, Compton dominance, black hole mass, accretion disk luminosity, and Eddington ratio.
AI.conclusion: Gamma-ray variability in jetted AGNs is likely governed by diffusive shock acceleration; the emission region is located beyond the BLR, possibly associated with the dusty torus; both jet activity and accretion processes contribute to gamma-ray variability.

title: Revisiting the mass metallicity relation and the fundamental metallicity relation of dwarf galaxies at cosmic noon with NIRISS
comment: resubmitted after addressing the referee report
summary: We extend the stellar-mass gas-phase metallicity relation (MZR) at $z = 1.1-3.4$ down to the extremely low-mass regime using 183 galaxies with $\log(M_*/M_\odot) = 6.3-10.2$, based on deep JWST/NIRISS slitless spectroscopy from the NGDEEP program. The derived MZR is in excellent agreement with our previous result from 50 galaxies in the GLASS-JWST sample, underscoring the robustness and universality of this relation. Together, these datasets constitute the largest sample of dwarf galaxies yet obtained with NIRISS. The observed MZR slope, $β\simeq0.24\pm0.03$, remains constant across nearly four orders of magnitude in stellar mass. Analytical modeling of the metal-loading factor of outflows ($ζ_\textrm{out}$) indicates that, at $M_*\lesssim10^8M_\odot$, $ζ_\textrm{out}$ becomes progressively less dominant than the gas fraction ($μ_\textrm{gas}$) in regulating the MZR slope. Using this enlarged NIRISS sample, we further test the existence of the fundamental metallicity relation (FMR). We find no robust evidence for an additional SFR dependence beyond the MZR, nor any reduction in metallicity scatter when SFR is included. Examination of systematic uncertainties in \oh, $M_*$ and SFR suggests that the MZR slope ($β\sim0.22$) is robust, and that different assumptions about the strong-line calibrations or star-formation history (SFH) of the galaxies change the slope by less than 1-$σ$. At the current depth of the NIRISS data, evidence for an FMR among high-redshift dwarf galaxies remains inconclusive, highlighting the need for larger samples, and deeper observations.

AI.tldr: Using JWST/NIRISS data from 183 galaxies at z=1.1-3.4, this paper extends the stellar mass-metallicity relation (MZR) down to log(M*/M⊙)=6.3, finds a constant slope β≈0.24 across nearly 4 dex in mass, shows that the metal-loading factor of outflows becomes less dominant than gas fraction at low masses, and finds no robust evidence for a fundamental metallicity relation (FMR) among high-redshift dwarf galaxies.
AI.motivation: To extend the stellar-mass gas-phase metallicity relation (MZR) to the extremely low-mass regime at high redshift (z=1.1-3.4) and test the existence of the fundamental metallicity relation (FMR) using deep JWST/NIRISS observations, addressing whether additional SFR dependence exists beyond the MZR.
AI.method: Analyzed 183 galaxies (log(M*/M⊙)=6.3-10.2) from deep JWST/NIRISS slitless spectroscopy (NGDEEP program), combined with 50 galaxies from GLASS-JWST. Used analytical modeling of the metal-loading factor (ζ_out) and gas fraction (μ_gas) to understand MZR slope regulation. Tested FMR by examining SFR dependence and scatter reduction. Assessed systematic uncertainties in O/H, M*, and SFR through varying strong-line calibrations and star-formation history assumptions.
AI.result: MZR slope β≈0.24±0.03 is constant across ~4 dex in stellar mass. At M*≲10^8 M⊙, ζ_out becomes less dominant than μ_gas in regulating the MZR slope. No robust evidence for an FMR; no additional SFR dependence or reduced scatter when SFR is included. MZR slope (β~0.22) is robust to systematic uncertainties (changes <1σ). Evidence for FMR among high-z dwarf galaxies remains inconclusive.
AI.conclusion: The MZR is robust and universal down to extremely low stellar masses at high redshift, with a constant slope regulated increasingly by gas fraction rather than outflows at low masses. The FMR remains unconfirmed for high-redshift dwarf galaxies with current data depth, necessitating larger samples and deeper observations.

title: Relativistic Scattering in the Funnel of Cygnus X-3
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Cygnus X-3 presents significant challenges to standard accretion models. Recent polarimetric observations by IXPE reveal high polarization degrees (PD) in the hard state ($\sim 23\%$) and unexpectedly significant polarization in the soft state ($\sim 12\%$), which are difficult to reconcile with static scattering models at low inclination ($i \approx 30^\circ$). We present a relativistic scattering model within a funnel-shaped geometry that resolves this discrepancy. We show that a single funnel-outflow configuration with variable bulk velocity $β$ can reproduce both polarization states, with lower velocities ($β\approx 0$) yielding $\sim 12\%$ polarization (soft state) and mildly relativistic velocities ($β\lesssim 0.4$) producing $\sim 23\%$ polarization (hard state) at $i \approx 30^\circ$ for half funnel opening angles of $\sim 13^\circ$-$16^\circ$. Relativistic aberration modifies the effective scattering angle in the comoving frame, enhancing polarization in the hard state while recovering the static limit in the soft state. The model also yields a consistent estimate of the intrinsic luminosity, of order $\sim 10^{40}$ erg s$^{-1}$, supporting a super-Eddington interpretation. This framework provides a unified explanation of the observed polarization properties of Cygnus X-3.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves the Cygnus X-3 polarization puzzle using a relativistic scattering model with a funnel-shaped outflow, where variable bulk velocity (static for soft state, mildly relativistic for hard state) explains the observed polarization degrees (~12% vs ~23%) at low inclination, also supporting super-Eddington luminosity.
AI.motivation: Cygnus X-3's observed polarization degrees (~23% in hard state, ~12% in soft state) contradict static scattering models at low inclination (~30°), motivating the need for a new theoretical framework.
AI.method: A relativistic scattering model within a funnel-shaped outflow geometry is developed, with variable bulk velocity β (0 to ~0.4) to transition between soft and hard states, incorporating relativistic aberration effects on effective scattering angles.
AI.result: Lower velocities (β≈0) yield ~12% PD (soft state); mildly relativistic velocities (β≲0.4) yield ~23% PD (hard state) at i≈30° for half-opening angles ~13°-16°. Intrinsic luminosity estimated at ~10^40 erg/s, consistent with super-Eddington accretion.
AI.conclusion: A single funnel-outflow configuration with variable bulk velocity provides a unified explanation for Cygnus X-3's polarization properties across spectral states.

title: Evolution of compressed clouds formed by filament coalescence. I. Oblique collisions
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, Accepted to Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan (PASJ)
summary: Stars are thought to form predominantly within filamentary molecular clouds. Recent studies have suggested that active star formation, including the formation of stellar clusters and massive stars, occurs within so-called "hub" structures, where multiple filaments converge. Understanding the formation and evolution of such hub-filament systems is therefore essential for unveiling the physical processes responsible for cluster and massive star formation, although the full picture remains incomplete. To address this, we have focused on filament-filament collisions as a potential formation mechanism of the hubs. In this study, we investigate the fundamental evolutionary processes of oblique collisions between two magnetized filaments using three-dimensional ideal magnetohydrodynamical simulations. As a model of initial filaments, we consider two identical finite-length magnetized filaments, varying the collision angle between their long axes, the collision velocity, which is set perpendicular to the long axes, and the initial line mass. We find that as the collision angle decreases from orthogonal to parallel, the compressed cloud becomes more prone to gravitational collapse. In addition, the instability of the post-collision compressed cloud can be explained by its energy balance. Specifically, if the absolute value of the gravitational energy exceeds the sum of the kinetic, thermal, and magnetic energies immediately after the collision, the cloud undergoes gravitational collapse. Conversely, if the gravitational energy is smaller, the cloud expands. In addition, we estimate the upper limit of the collision velocity that enables hub-filament formation and identify the collision conditions favorable for massive star formation.

AI.tldr: This study uses 3D ideal MHD simulations to investigate oblique collisions between two magnetized filaments as a formation mechanism for hub-filament systems, finding that smaller collision angles promote gravitational collapse, with collapse determined by whether gravitational energy exceeds the sum of kinetic, thermal, and magnetic energies post-collision, and identifying favorable conditions for massive star formation.
AI.motivation: Hub-filament systems are thought to be crucial sites for cluster and massive star formation, but their formation mechanism remains incompletely understood. This study aims to investigate filament-filament collisions as a potential formation pathway.
AI.method: Three-dimensional ideal magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) simulations of oblique collisions between two identical finite-length magnetized filaments, varying collision angle, collision velocity (perpendicular to long axes), and initial line mass.
AI.result: Smaller collision angles (from orthogonal to parallel) make the compressed cloud more prone to gravitational collapse. The instability of the post-collision cloud is governed by energy balance: collapse occurs when gravitational energy exceeds the sum of kinetic, thermal, and magnetic energies; otherwise, the cloud expands.
AI.conclusion: The study provides an upper limit on collision velocity for hub-filament formation and identifies favorable collision conditions for massive star formation, advancing understanding of how hub structures and stellar clusters form via filament interactions.

title: Superfluid fraction in the crystalline crust of a neutron star: role of quantum zero-point motion of ions
comment: 15 pages
summary: The suppression of the neutron superfluid fraction in the inner crust of a cold neutron star is mitigated by the quantum zero-point motion of ions about their equilibrium position. In turn, the crustal dynamics is altered by the presence of the neutron superfluid. These effects are studied self-consistently to assess the validity of the usual assumption of a perfect rigid lattice. To this end, fully three-dimensional band-structure calculations of the superfluid fraction are carried out in the weak-coupling approximation, considering body- and face-centered cubic lattices. In both cases, the superfluid fraction is still found to be strongly suppressed in the intermediate region of the inner crust. In turn, the effective mass of the ions is dramatically increased, thus further damping the ion fluctuations. These results are of relevance for the rotational and thermal evolutions of neutron stars.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how the quantum zero-point motion of ions reduces the suppression of neutron superfluidity in the inner crust of cold neutron stars, and how the resulting superfluid fraction feeds back to increase the effective ion mass, damping ion fluctuations. Using 3D band-structure calculations for BCC and FCC lattices, the authors find strong superfluid suppression in the intermediate crust region and a significant increase in ion effective mass, relevant to neutron star rotational and thermal evolution.
AI.motivation: To assess the validity of the assumption of a perfect rigid lattice in the inner crust of neutron stars and to self-consistently study the interplay between neutron superfluid suppression and ionic quantum zero-point motion.
AI.method: Fully three-dimensional band-structure calculations of the superfluid fraction in the weak-coupling approximation, considering body-centered and face-centered cubic lattices.
AI.result: The superfluid fraction remains strongly suppressed in the intermediate region of the inner crust for both lattice types, and the effective mass of ions is dramatically increased, further damping ion fluctuations.
AI.conclusion: The interplay between superfluid suppression and ion dynamics is significant; the results have implications for the rotational and thermal evolution of neutron stars.

title: Robustness Analysis of USmorph: II. Optimizing Feature Extraction, Dimensionality Reduction, and Clustering for Unsupervised Galaxy Morphology Classification
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables; accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: We conduct a systematic robustness analysis of the unsupervised machine learning module within the hybrid framework \texttt{USmorph}. This module automatically discovers morphological structures from large-scale galaxy images, forming the foundation of the complete classification workflow. We evaluate five pre-trained models for feature extraction and identify an ImageNet-pretrained AlexNet as the most effective for capturing discriminative morphological features. UMAP is chosen for dimensionality reduction due to its optimal balance between preserving high-dimensional structure and computational efficiency. To enhance clustering stability, we propose a Bagging-based multi-cluster voting scheme, which significantly improves label consistency and cluster purity. We compare the convergence, scalability, and quality of five clustering algorithms, finding that the Bagging voting scheme has the best performance with the combination of K-means, Birch, and Agg. A bagging clustering number of $K=16$ is used to achieve the optimal balance between classification granularity and manual validation efficiency. Our tests show that: (1) the t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) reveals clear, compact cluster boundaries in low-dimensional space with strong feature separability; (2) the morphology classification results align with galaxy evolution theory, showing physically plausible distributions of different types in parameter space. These results demonstrate the technical robustness and scientific credibility of \texttt{USmorph}, establishing it as a reliable method for automated morphological classification in future large-scale surveys such as the China Space Station Telescope (CSST) mission.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates the robustness of the unsupervised machine learning module in the USmorph framework for galaxy morphology classification. It identifies ImageNet-pretrained AlexNet as the best feature extractor, UMAP for dimensionality reduction, and proposes a Bagging-based multi-cluster voting scheme that improves clustering stability. The optimal configuration (K=16 with K-means, Birch, and Agg) yields physically plausible morphological classifications consistent with galaxy evolution theory.
AI.motivation: To systematically assess the robustness of the unsupervised learning pipeline in USmorph, ensuring its reliability for automated morphological classification in future large-scale galaxy surveys such as the CSST mission.
AI.method: Evaluated five pre-trained models for feature extraction; selected ImageNet-pretrained AlexNet as best; used UMAP for dimensionality reduction; proposed a Bagging-based multi-cluster voting scheme; compared five clustering algorithms for convergence, scalability, and quality; used K=16 bagging clustering with K-means, Birch, and Agg combination.
AI.result: t-SNE reveals clear, compact cluster boundaries with strong feature separability; morphology classifications align with galaxy evolution theory, showing physically plausible parameter-space distributions.
AI.conclusion: USmorph demonstrates technical robustness and scientific credibility, establishing it as a reliable method for automated morphological classification in future large-scale surveys like the CSST mission.

title: Lack of Significant Orbital-Phase Locking in the Active Phases of the Recurrent Nova T CrB
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, Submitted to The Astrophysical Journal (ApJ)
summary: T Coronae Borealis (T CrB) is a symbiotic recurrent nova (RN) that exhibits both nova eruptions and long-term active phases resembling superoutbursts and normal outbursts. Motivated by proposed connections between these events and the binary orbit, we test whether the onset, maximum, or termination of the active phases is locked to orbital phase. We use long-term optical $B$- and $V$-band light curves from the American Association of Variable Stars Observers (AAVSO) International Database and historical photometry from the literature. We measure the onset, maximum, and termination times of superoutbursts and normal outbursts and convert these times to orbital phase. We test the resulting circular distributions with Kuiper and Watson statistics. We find no statistically significant orbital-phase locking. The maxima and termination are consistent with a uniform phase distribution. The smallest probabilities occur for the normal-outburst onset phases ($p_{\rm MC}=0.083$ for the Kuiper statistic and $p_{\rm MC}=0.079$ for the Watson statistic), but these values do not satisfy either a commonly used $p<0.05$ criterion or a $3σ$ criterion ($p=0.0027$). We therefore treat any apparent onset preference as a non-detection. The four historical nova eruptions likewise do not provide robust evidence for a unique ignition phase once the small sample size, historical date uncertainties, and long-term period changes are considered. The two known secondary eruptions occurred at similar phases, but two events are insufficient to establish an orbital-geometry connection. Overall, the active phases of T CrB appear to be governed primarily by accretion-disk physics rather than by a fixed binary phase.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether the active phases (superoutbursts, normal outbursts, and nova eruptions) of the recurrent symbiotic nova T Coronae Borealis are locked to orbital phase, finding no statistically significant phase locking and concluding that accretion-disk physics, not binary phase, primarily governs these events.
AI.motivation: To test whether the onset, maximum, or termination of T CrB's active phases (superoutbursts, normal outbursts, and nova eruptions) are locked to orbital phase, motivated by proposed connections between these events and the binary orbit.
AI.method: Analyzed long-term optical B- and V-band light curves from AAVSO and historical photometry; measured onset, maximum, and termination times of superoutbursts and normal outbursts; converted to orbital phase; tested circular distributions using Kuiper and Watson statistics with Monte Carlo significance estimates.
AI.result: No statistically significant orbital-phase locking found. Normal-outburst onset phases yielded marginal p-values (Kuiper p_MC=0.083, Watson p_MC=0.079), failing both p<0.05 and 3σ criteria. Historical nova eruptions and secondary eruptions also lacked robust evidence for orbital-phase dependence.
AI.conclusion: The active phases of T CrB appear to be governed primarily by accretion-disk physics rather than by a fixed binary phase.

title: The TNG50-SKIRT Atlas: Multi-wavelength nonparametric galaxy morphology
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Context: Galaxy morphology is a fundamental property to describe galaxy evolution. However, the observed morphology of a particular galaxy may depend on the observed wavelength. Aims: Our aim is to investigate the wavelength dependence and the effect of dust attenuation on nonparametric morphology indicators. Methods: We use the TNG50-SKIRT Atlas, an atlas of synthetic UV to near-infrared (NIR) broadband images for a complete stellar-mass-selected sample of 1154 galaxies extracted from the TNG50 cosmological simulation at $z = 0$. For each image, we calculate four nonparametric morphology indicators using the StatMorph code. Results: We find that the known correlations between the stellar mass and the morphological parameters measured in the optical, together with the Gini-$M_{20}$, concentration-Gini, and concentration-$M_{20}$ planes, are fully consistent with observational data. However, nonparametric morphological indicators change significantly with wavelength and that this wavelength dependence is stronger for disc-dominated than for bulge-dominated galaxies. The wavelength dependence of the morphology of our simulated TNG50 galaxies is consistent with measurements of local galaxies from the SINGS survey. We demonstrate that the effect of dust attenuation on nonparametric morphology indicators is modest across the full galaxy population but can be significant for individual galaxies.

AI.tldr: Using the TNG50-SKIRT Atlas of 1154 simulated galaxies, this paper investigates how nonparametric morphology indicators change with wavelength and dust attenuation, finding wavelength dependence stronger in disk-dominated galaxies and modest dust effects across the population but significant for individual galaxies.
AI.motivation: To investigate the wavelength dependence and the effect of dust attenuation on nonparametric morphology indicators, given that observed galaxy morphology may vary with wavelength.
AI.method: Using the TNG50-SKIRT Atlas (synthetic UV-to-NIR broadband images for 1154 stellar-mass-selected galaxies from TNG50 at z=0) and calculating four nonparametric morphology indicators with the StatMorph code.
AI.result: (1) Stellar mass-morphology correlations and Gini-M20, concentration-Gini, and concentration-M20 planes are consistent with observations. (2) Morphological indicators change significantly with wavelength, stronger for disk-dominated than bulge-dominated galaxies. (3) Wavelength dependence is consistent with SINGS survey measurements. (4) Dust attenuation has modest effects across the population but can be significant for individual galaxies.
AI.conclusion: Nonparametric morphology indicators are wavelength-dependent, especially for disk-dominated galaxies, and dust attenuation effects are modest on average but non-negligible for individual cases.

title: The radio emission from radiative filaments of Cygnus Loop
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, ApJ accepted
summary: The Galactic supernova remnant (SNR) Cygnus Loop emerges as an ideal laboratory for analyzing the different radiation mechanisms, as well as the particle acceleration mechanisms at different types of shocks. In order to determine radio spectral indices of non-radiative and radiative filaments in Cygnus Loop, we observed previously optically analyzed filaments with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (VLA). At 1 and 5 GHz, we detected only radiative filaments in the field of view. Non-radiative optical filaments are also present, but were not detected in radio. Contrary to the expected non-thermal spectral slopes characteristic of SNRs, we instead observed spectral slopes characteristic of the thermal radiation mechanism from the radiative filaments in Cygnus Loop. These evolutionary older parts of Cygnus Loop radiate at radio frequencies predominantly via the thermal bremsstrahlung mechanism, and in that sense their emission more closely resembles the radio emission of HII regions rather than the radio emission of SNRs.

AI.tldr: Radio observations of the Cygnus Loop SNR at 1 and 5 GHz detected only radiative (but not non-radiative) filaments, revealing thermal bremsstrahlung (rather than non-thermal synchrotron) emission with spectral slopes resembling HII regions instead of typical SNRs.
AI.motivation: To determine radio spectral indices of different types of shock filaments (non-radiative vs. radiative) in the Cygnus Loop SNR, using previously optically characterized filaments as targets.
AI.method: VLA observations at 1 and 5 GHz targeting previously identified optically analyzed filaments in the Cygnus Loop SNR, comparing radio detection and spectral indices between non-radiative and radiative filaments.
AI.result: Only radiative filaments were detected in radio; non-radiative optical filaments remained undetected. The detected radiative filaments exhibited thermal bremsstrahlung spectral slopes rather than the non-thermal slopes typical of SNRs.
AI.conclusion: Older, evolved radiative regions of the Cygnus Loop emit at radio frequencies predominantly via thermal bremsstrahlung, more akin to HII region radio emission than classical SNR non-thermal emission.

title: Difference Between Half-mass Radius and Half-light Radius of Galaxies at 0.2 $< z <$ 2.5 Revealed by JWST/NIRCam Data
comment: 18 pages, 14 figures, 3 tables; published in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Using JWST observations in CANDELS fields, we measure the half-light radius ($r_{\rm e,light}$) and half-mass radius ($r_{\rm e,mass}$) for 14,333 galaxies with stellar masses $M_* > 10^9 M_\odot$ at redshifts $0.2 < z < 2.5$. To investigate the difference between $r_{\rm e,light}$ and $r_{\rm e,mass}$, we find that $r_{\rm e,light}$ is larger than $r_{\rm e,mass}$ for both quiescent galaxies (QGs) and star-forming galaxies (SFGs). Moreover, the difference between these two radii is clearly correlated with galaxy stellar mass, $r_{\rm e,light}$, and the rest-frame $U - V$ color. When examining the evolution of the $r_{\rm e,mass}/r_{\rm e,light}$ ratio, we observe a significant increase for SFGs at $z > 1.7$. In contrast, no clear increase is observed for QGs at $z > 1$, though a slight decreasing trend is seen between $0.2 < z < 1.0$. By fitting a linear relationship between galaxy size and stellar mass, we find that the slope for $r_{\rm e,light}$ is $\sim$ 0.1 to 0.3 dex larger than that for $r_{\rm e,mass}$. In terms of galaxy size evolution at a fixed stellar mass, the $r_{\rm e,mass}$ of QGs increases by a factor of $\sim$ 3 to 5 from $z \sim 2.5$ to $z \sim 0.2$. In contrast, the $r_{\rm e,mass}$ of SFGs increases by a factor of approximately 2 over the same redshift range, with this growth trend closely following that of their $r_{\rm e,light}$. These results indicate that previous insights into galaxy evolution based on $r_{\rm e,light}$ remain valid when considering $r_{\rm e,mass}$, although the specific slopes show some variations.

AI.tldr: Using JWST CANDELS data for 14,333 galaxies (z=0.2–2.5), this paper compares half-light radius (r_e,light) and half-mass radius (r_e,mass), finding r_e,light > r_e,mass for both quiescent and star-forming galaxies. The radius ratio evolves differently for QGs vs SFGs, and the mass–size relation slope is steeper for light-based sizes. Overall, previous evolutionary insights from light radii remain valid, albeit with quantitative differences in slopes.
AI.motivation: To investigate the difference between half-light and half-mass radii in galaxies across cosmic time, and to assess whether previous conclusions about galaxy size evolution based on light radii remain valid when using mass-based sizes.
