AI.method: JWST observations in CANDELS fields; measured half-light radius (r_e,light) and half-mass radius (r_e,mass) for 14,333 galaxies with M* > 10^9 M⊙ at 0.2 < z < 2.5; compared radii and analyzed their dependence on stellar mass, color, and redshift; fitted linear mass–size relations; traced evolutionary trends for quiescent and star-forming galaxies separately.
AI.result: (1) r_e,light > r_e,mass for both QGs and SFGs; (2) the radius difference correlates with stellar mass, r_e,light, and U−V color; (3) r_e,mass/r_e,light ratio increases significantly for SFGs at z>1.7, but shows no clear increase (slight decline at 0.2<z<1.0) for QGs; (4) mass–size slope for r_e,light is ~0.1–0.3 dex steeper than for r_e,mass; (5) at fixed mass, r_e,mass of QGs grows ~3–5× from z~2.5 to 0.2, while SFGs grow ~2×, following their light-radius evolution.
AI.conclusion: Previous galaxy evolution insights based on r_e,light remain valid when using r_e,mass, though specific slopes differ quantitatively.

title: Chandra X-ray Observations of the Pulsar Wind Nebula within CTA 1
comment: Submitted to ApJ, 18 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables
summary: We present deep Chandra observations of the pulsar wind nebula (PWN) powered by PSR J0007+7303 in the composite supernova remnant CTA 1. The merged ACIS image shows a $\sim20''$ jet extending south of the pulsar and bending toward the southwest, a faint counter-jet to the north, and a compact torus oriented approximately perpendicular to the jet axis. Using an archival observation from 2003 we perform relative astrometry over a $\sim20$ yr baseline and constrain the pulsar's transverse velocity to $\lesssim 200~\mathrm{km~s^{-1}}$ at the distance of 1.4 kpc at 95% confidence. Spatially resolved spectroscopy shows hard spectra for the jet and torus (photon indicies $Γ\approx 1.2-1.4$) and a softer spectrum for the extended nebula ($Γ= 1.85 \pm 0.11$), indicating minimal radiative cooling in the compact regions. Modeling of the torus, associated with the termination shock, as an inclined circle yields a viewing angle $ζ\approx 50^\circ$. The outer gap and two-pole caustic pulsar emission models then imply a moderate magnetic inclination ($α\sim 20^\circ$-$70^\circ$). Broadband spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling from radio to PeV $γ$-rays for a one-zone leptonic scenario yields a low magnetic field ($B \approx 1.4$-$3.2~μ\mathrm{G}$) and a high electron cutoff energy ($E_{\rm cut} \sim 0.2$-$0.3~\mathrm{PeV}$), indicating that the magnetic field decreases rapidly outside of the compact nebula. These results establish CTA 1 as a young, low X-ray efficiency PWN with a hard injection spectrum capable of accelerating particles to PeV energies.

AI.tldr: Deep Chandra observations of PSR J0007+7303's PWN in CTA 1 reveal a jet, counter-jet, and torus structure. The pulsar's transverse velocity is ≤200 km/s. The torus viewing angle is ~50°, with magnetic inclination α~20°-70°. SED modeling shows a low magnetic field (1.4-3.2 μG) and high electron cutoff energy (0.2-0.3 PeV), establishing CTA 1 as a young PWN capable of accelerating particles to PeV energies.
AI.motivation: To study the structure, kinematics, and emission properties of the pulsar wind nebula powered by PSR J0007+7303 in the composite supernova remnant CTA 1, and to understand particle acceleration mechanisms up to PeV energies.
AI.method: Deep Chandra ACIS X-ray observations, relative astrometry over ~20 yr baseline, spatially resolved spectroscopy, geometric modeling of the torus as an inclined circle, outer gap and two-pole caustic pulsar emission models, and one-zone leptonic broadband SED modeling from radio to PeV γ-rays.
AI.result: Discovered a ~20" southward-extending jet bending southwest, a faint northward counter-jet, and a compact torus perpendicular to the jet axis. Pulsar transverse velocity ≤200 km/s at 1.4 kpc. Jet/torus spectra hard (Γ≈1.2-1.4), extended nebula softer (Γ=1.85±0.11). Viewing angle ζ≈50°, magnetic inclination α~20°-70°. Magnetic field B≈1.4-3.2 μG, electron cutoff E_cut~0.2-0.3 PeV.
AI.conclusion: CTA 1 is a young, low X-ray efficiency PWN with a hard injection spectrum, capable of accelerating particles to PeV energies. The magnetic field decreases rapidly outside the compact nebula, and minimal radiative cooling occurs in the compact regions.

title: On the Possibility of an Extragalactic Positron Annihilation Signal
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables, accepted in A&A
summary: With 20 years of INTEGRAL/SPI observations, Yoneda et al. (2025) created the most detailed map of the positron annihilation line at 511keV. While central bulge and extended disk are readily recognised in this map, several hotspots at high latitude regions may either be imaging artefacts or true signals. We discuss the possibility of extragalactic positron annihilation signals from hotspots in this map. We also calculate a cosmological positron annihilation signal as a contribution to the Cosmic Gamma-ray Background (CGB). For this investigation, we compare 511 keV emission hotspots away from the Galactic plane with a high velocity cloud column density map as well as with the catalogue of Local Volume Galaxies (LVGs) up to 25 Mpc. We find that in particular the Magellanic Stream in the southern and Complex C in the northern sky matches the brightest hotspots, which may indicate a higher positron production rate inside the Milky Way than measured from the Galactic interstellar medium alone, of $10^{44}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. In addition, we can explain other hotspots by the cumulative effect of LVGs in the selected regions. The CGB contribution from positron annihilation might be sub-dominant on the per-cent level. However, depending on the true intrinsic annihilation spectrum, in particular depending on the positron injection energy for in-flight annihilation and the star formation rate per galaxy, a much higher imprint beyond 10% is possible above several MeV. If these findings turn out to be true, next generation MeV telescopes will, for the first time, identify individual extragalactic 511 keV sources. In particular, several dwarf spheroidal galaxies with fluxes of up to $(1$-$2) \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{ph\,cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, the galaxies M31 and M33, as well as some of their satellites, with potentially several $10^{-6}\,\mathrm{ph\,cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, each, may be detected.

AI.tldr: Yoneda et al. (2025) analyze 20 years of INTEGRAL/SPI data on the 511 keV positron annihilation line. They find that hotspots at high latitudes partly align with the Magellanic Stream and Complex C, suggesting a higher Galactic positron production rate (10^44 s^-1). Other hotspots may come from Local Volume Galaxies. The cosmological contribution to the Cosmic Gamma-ray Background is sub-dominant (~1%) but could exceed 10% above several MeV depending on injection energy and star formation rate. Future MeV telescopes might detect individual extragalactic 511 keV sources like dwarf spheroidals, M31, and M33.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether high-latitude 511 keV hotspots in the INTEGRAL/SPI map are extragalactic positron annihilation signals, and to estimate the cosmological contribution of positron annihilation to the Cosmic Gamma-ray Background (CGB).
AI.method: Comparison of 511 keV emission hotspots away from the Galactic plane with HVC column density maps and the catalogue of Local Volume Galaxies (LVGs) up to 25 Mpc, plus calculation of the cosmological positron annihilation signal as a CGB component.
AI.result: The Magellanic Stream and Complex C match the brightest hotspots, suggesting a Galactic positron production rate of 10^44 s^-1. Other hotspots are explainable by cumulative LVG emission. CGB contribution is sub-dominant (~1%) but can exceed 10% above several MeV depending on spectrum assumptions.
AI.conclusion: If confirmed, next-generation MeV telescopes could detect individual extragalactic 511 keV sources, including dwarf spheroidal galaxies (flux ~1-2×10^-5 ph cm^-2 s^-1) and M31/M33 (~several ×10^-6 ph cm^-2 s^-1).

title: Dawn of the Milky Way disk: Determination of when a rotationally supported disk appears and dating the spin-up of the disk
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures. Paper accepted by ApJLetters
summary: Spiral galaxies, like the Milky Way, transform at some point in time into a rotationally supported system. Using an extant data-set consisting of 319 835 sub-giants from LAMOST with precise ages from the literature, we determine, for the first time the age when the Milky Way disk spins up, i.e. when the mean circular velocity changes from halo-like to disk-like. We find in concordance previous studies that the spin-up takes place for -1.25 < [Fe/H] <- 0.9 and we can date this transition to a mean age of 12.1 +/- 2.8 Gyr (median age 12.4 Gyr). We further study when the disk became rotationally supported, i.e. when the ordered, disky motion dominates over the random motions. We find that this happens for $-1.25<$[Fe/H]$<-1$. The transition is very rapid in age. This gives support to that the spin-up seen in this and other works genuinely traces the motion to a rotationally supported disk, which has not previously been shown. These transitions are traced by the high-alpha stars. while the low-alpha stars do not spin-up but start directly at approximately the circular velocity seen for the Sun today. The low-alpha disk is rotationally supported with no transition period in [Fe/H] or in age.

AI.tldr: Using LAMOST data of 319,835 sub-giants with precise ages, the Milky Way disk spin-up occurs at [Fe/H] ~ -1.25 to -0.9, with a mean age of 12.1 Gyr, and the transition to rotational support happens rapidly at [Fe/H] ~ -1.25 to -1, traced by high-alpha stars, while low-alpha stars show no spin-up and are already rotationally supported.
AI.motivation: To determine when the Milky Way disk spins up and becomes rotationally supported, using precise stellar ages from a large sub-giant sample, and to clarify whether the spin-up genuinely traces the transition to a rotationally supported disk, which had not been previously established.
AI.method: Analysis of 319,835 sub-giant stars from LAMOST with precise ages from the literature; measurement of mean circular velocity changes as a function of metallicity and age to identify the spin-up epoch and the transition to rotational support.
AI.result: Spin-up occurs at -1.25 < [Fe/H] < -0.9 with mean age 12.1 ± 2.8 Gyr (median 12.4 Gyr). Rotational support transition happens at -1.25 < [Fe/H] < -1, very rapidly in age, traced by high-alpha stars. Low-alpha stars show no spin-up and are already rotationally supported at approximately the local circular velocity.
AI.conclusion: The Milky Way disk experienced a rapid spin-up and transition to rotational support in its early history (~12 Gyr ago), traced by high-alpha stars, while the low-alpha disk formed already rotationally supported.

title: B-Fields and Star Formation across Scales with TRAO (B-FROST): CO Abundances, Dynamics and Relative Orientations in the Translucent High Latitude Cloud MBM12
comment: 21 pages, 16 figures, accepted in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: In our Galaxy, the average star formation efficiency is of the order of a few percent. We investigated the high-latitude molecular cloud MBM12 as part of the B-fields and star formation across scales (B-FROST) survey with the Taeduk Radio Astronomical Observatory (TRAO) to assess why star formation activity in MBM12 is low. We combine {\it Herschel}-based, locally $κ_ν$-calibrated $N$(H$_2$) estimates with $^{12}$CO and $^{13}$CO ($J=1-0$) observations (2.5$^\circ \times$3$^\circ$ at 48$''$) to map $N$(CO), $X$(CO), and [CO/H$_2$], compute multi-scale $α_{\rm vir}$ and mass-size scaling laws from dendrograms, and derive the histogram of relative orientations from {\it Planck} dust polarisation. We identify four main regions based on velocities that have H$_2$ column densities ranging from $2\times10^{20}$ cm$^{-2} - 1.3\times10^{22}$ cm$^{-2}$. The average $X$(CO) is close to the galactic average, with variations below $X_{\rm Gal}$ from collisional de-excitation in low-density gas, and above $X_{\rm Gal}$ from CO photodissociation at cloud edges. The hierarchical structures follow a broken power law mass-size relation $M=AR^α$. The values of $α_{\rm vir}$ ranged from $3-60$, with the smallest values at 0.1 pc scales. The mass-size relations for the structures with the lowest $α_{\rm vir}$ have scaling factors $A$ three times larger than those of high $α_{\rm vir}$ structures, indicating external pressure one order of magnitude larger. We found a transition of parallel to perpendicular between column density structures and magnetic field orientations at $N$(H$_2$) $= 4.5 \times 10^{21}$ cm$^{-2}$. We provide the first integrated chemical, dynamical, and magnetic field analysis of MBM12. Scale-dependent mass-size and virial analysis can further constrain the role of external pressure in regulating the star formation efficiency.

AI.tldr: Study of MBM12 molecular cloud shows low star formation efficiency due to external pressure and magnetic fields, with virial parameters of 3-60, a transition in magnetic field alignment at N(H₂)=4.5×10²¹ cm⁻², and hierarchical mass-size relations indicating external pressure one order of magnitude larger in low-virial structures.
AI.motivation: To understand why star formation activity in the high-latitude molecular cloud MBM12 is low despite having H₂ column densities up to 1.3×10²² cm⁻², by investigating the roles of external pressure and magnetic fields.
AI.method: Combined Herschel-based κ_ν-calibrated N(H₂) estimates with TRAO ¹²CO and ¹³CO (J=1-0) observations (2.5°×3° at 48″) to map N(CO), X(CO), and [CO/H₂]; computed multi-scale α_vir and mass-size scaling laws from dendrograms; derived relative orientation histograms from Planck dust polarization.
AI.result: Identified four velocity-defined regions with N(H₂)=2×10²⁰-1.3×10²² cm⁻². X(CO) varies near Galactic average. Hierarchical structures follow broken power-law mass-size relation. α_vir ranges 3-60, lowest at 0.1 pc scales. Low-α_vir structures have 3× larger scaling factor A, indicating 10× larger external pressure. Magnetic field orientation transitions from parallel to perpendicular at N(H₂)=4.5×10²¹ cm⁻².
AI.conclusion: First integrated chemical, dynamical, and magnetic field analysis of MBM12. Scale-dependent mass-size and virial analysis can further constrain how external pressure regulates star formation efficiency.

title: FR0 radio galaxy jets -- I. linking jet dynamics and high-energy emission in LEDA 55267 and LEDA 58287
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: Fanaroff-Riley type 0 (FR0) radio galaxies host anomalously compact jets whose disruption mechanism and high-energy emission remain poorly understood. We combine three-dimensional relativistic hydrodynamical (RHD) simulations with broadband spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling from radio to TeV energies, focusing on LEDA~55267 and LEDA~58287. Our simulations show that recollimation shocks trigger hydrodynamical instabilities that drive turbulence and rapid deceleration, preventing the jets from propagating beyond a few tens of parsecs and reproducing the observed compact radio morphology. Leptonic SED models adequately describe the observed emission up to GeV energies, but when simulated CTAO observations are included, statistical model comparison indicates strong evidence in favor of lepto-hadronic scenarios at TeV energies for both sources, a result that should be interpreted as a theoretical prediction to be tested by future observations. A leptonic analysis of the simulations reveals magnetized emitting regions with plasma beta parameters $β_{\rm p} \sim 10^{-5}$-$10^{-3}$, orders of magnitude below values reported for extended FRI jets, consistent with jets retaining the magnetization inherited from the launching region and providing a natural physical link between the compact jet dynamics and the lepto-hadronic emission.

AI.tldr: This paper uses 3D relativistic hydrodynamical simulations and SED modeling to show that recollimation shocks in FR0 radio galaxies trigger instabilities causing jet disruption within tens of parsecs, and that lepto-hadronic models are statistically preferred over leptonic models at TeV energies, with simulations revealing extremely low plasma beta values ($\beta_{\rm p} \sim 10^{-5}$-$10^{-3}$) linking compact jet dynamics to high-energy emission.
AI.motivation: To understand the disruption mechanism of anomalously compact jets in FR0 radio galaxies and to investigate their high-energy (TeV) emission, which remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Combined 3D relativistic hydrodynamical (RHD) simulations with broadband spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling from radio to TeV energies, focusing on two sources (LEDA 55267 and LEDA 58287). Included statistical model comparison using simulated CTAO observations to test leptonic vs. lepto-hadronic scenarios.
AI.result: Recollimation shocks trigger hydrodynamical instabilities that drive turbulence and rapid deceleration, limiting jets to tens of parsecs. Leptonic models describe emission up to GeV energies, but lepto-hadronic scenarios are statistically favored at TeV energies. Simulations show plasma beta parameters $\beta_{\rm p} \sim 10^{-5}$-$10^{-3}$, much lower than in extended FRI jets.
AI.conclusion: FR0 jets retain magnetization from the launching region, providing a physical link between compact jet dynamics and lepto-hadronic TeV emission. The lepto-hadronic preference is a theoretical prediction to be tested by future CTAO observations.

title: Detection of a dark matter subhalo in the strongly lensed system PJ011646
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures
summary: We present a strong lensing analysis of the system PJ011646 using high-resolution ($\sim$0.1 arcsec) Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) dust-continuum observations to test for the presence of dark matter substructures. The lens mass distribution is modelled with an elliptical power law and third- and fourth-order multipoles (PL+MP; $m=3,4$), plus external shear. The multipoles have amplitudes of $\simeq$1.5 per cent of the convergence, consistent with nearby early-type galaxies, and improve the fit by $Δ\ln Z = 52.1$ relative to a pure PL model. Using this best-fitting macromodel, we perform a grid-based subhalo search in the image plane, parametrising the perturber as a spherical NFW. A subhalo in two locations in the image plane improves the fit by $Δ\ln Z>10$. Both correspond to the same location in the source plane, so they are partially degenerate; follow-up analysis suggests that only one is physically real. This is a subhalo of mass $M_{200} = {2.78}_{-0.66}^{+0.43} \times 10^{10} \, M_\odot$ and concentration $c_{200} = 30_{-7}^{+5}$, detected at $\sim$5.8$σ$ significance (relative to the PL+MP). This concentration is consistent with that expected for a typical tidally stripped Navarro-Frenk-White subhalo. The enclosed projected mass is most tightly constrained within a radius of 2 kpc, where we infer $M_{\rm sub} = {3.57}_{-0.14}^{+0.16}\times 10^9 \, M_\odot$. From grid cells consistent with no detection ($Δ\ln Z < 10$), we derive limits on the minimum subhalo mass that could have been detected at $3σ$ significance, finding $M_{200} \approx 8 \times 10^{8} \, M_\odot$ in the most sensitive regions of the lensed arcs. This demonstrates that ALMA continuum imaging at sub-arcsecond resolution can probe dark matter substructure in a mass regime where cold and warm dark matter models predict different abundances of subhalos.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a strong lensing analysis of PJ011646 using ALMA dust-continuum observations to detect dark matter substructure. The authors model the lens mass distribution with an elliptical power law plus multipoles (m=3,4) and external shear, then perform a grid-based subhalo search. They detect a subhalo of mass M200 = 2.78×10^10 M⊙ at ~5.8σ significance, with concentration c200 = 30, consistent with a tidally stripped NFW subhalo. The enclosed projected mass within 2 kpc is 3.57×10^9 M⊙. Detection limits reach M200 ≈ 8×10^8 M⊙ in sensitive regions, demonstrating ALMA's capability to probe dark matter substructure in a mass regime critical for distinguishing cold and warm dark matter models.
AI.motivation: To test for the presence of dark matter substructures in the lens system PJ011646 using high-resolution ALMA dust-continuum observations, probing a mass regime where cold and warm dark matter models predict different subhalo abundances.
AI.method: Strong lensing analysis with elliptical power law + multipoles (m=3,4) plus external shear for the macromodel; grid-based subhalo search in the image plane parametrizing perturbers as spherical NFW profiles; Bayesian model comparison using Δln Z.
AI.result: Detection of a subhalo at ~5.8σ significance with M200 = 2.78^{+0.43}_{-0.66}×10^10 M⊙ and c200 = 30^{+5}_{-7}, enclosed projected mass Msub = 3.57^{+0.16}_{-0.14}×10^9 M⊙ within 2 kpc. Detection limits reach M200 ≈ 8×10^8 M⊙ in sensitive regions.
AI.conclusion: ALMA continuum imaging at sub-arcsecond resolution can effectively probe dark matter substructure in a mass regime critical for distinguishing between cold and warm dark matter models.

title: Searching for links between energetic millisecond pulsars and repeating fast radio bursts
comment: Published in MNRAS
summary: The unexpected localization of the repeating FRB 20200120E to a globular cluster challenges conventional FRB models based on magnetars formed via core collapse. One alternative model suggests that FRB 20200120E is a millisecond pulsar (MSP) producing giant pulses (GPs). To test this hypothesis, we compared the characteristics of FRB 20200120E bursts with the GPs of the most energetic Galactic MSP known, M28A (PSR B1821$-$24A), using observations with the Parkes (Murriyang) telescope's Ultra Wideband Low-frequency (UWL) receiver. Our analysis provides insight into the spectral structure and frequency extent of M28A's GPs, revealing broad-band spectra spanning $700-4000$ MHz (in some cases) with complex spectral peaks. We find that known M28A GP characteristics persist at this bandwidth, such as durations, luminosities, periodicity, wait-time, and energy distribution. A sub-band search for narrow-band GPs yielded no detection of genuinely narrow-band GPs. However, we do find narrow-band spectral peaks of $\sim100$ MHz bandwidth, a similar scale observed for FRB 20200120E's bursts. Compared to FRB 20200120E's bursts, M28A's GPs have $50\times$ shorter durations, $10^5\times$ lower spectral luminosities, clear periodicity (vs. no periodicity), a purely Poissonian wait-time distribution (vs. quasi-Poissonian), and generally broad-band spectra with narrow-band peaks (vs. only narrow-band bursts). Both sources show a steep energy distribution and minor dispersion measure variability. Our study finds no strong links between M28A and FRB 20200120E. However, we cannot rule out the possibility that FRB 20200120E is a rare and unique type of MSP with no Galactic analogue. Furthermore, higher-cadence monitoring of M28A, for hundreds to thousands of hours, might reveal rare but extremely luminous pulses.

AI.tldr: The study compares FRB 20200120E bursts with giant pulses (GPs) from the Galactic millisecond pulsar M28A (PSB B1821−24A) using Parkes UWL observations. While both sources share steep energy distributions and minor DM variability, M28A's GPs have 50× shorter durations, 10⁵× lower spectral luminosities, clear periodicity, purely Poissonian wait-times, and broad-band spectra with narrow peaks—contrasting with FRB 20200120E's narrow-band bursts without periodicity. No strong links are found, but an exotic MSP origin for FRB 20200120E cannot be excluded.
AI.motivation: To test the hypothesis that FRB 20200120E—which localized to a globular cluster—could be a millisecond pulsar producing giant pulses, by comparing its burst properties to the most energetic known Galactic MSP, M28A.
AI.method: Observations of M28A with Parkes UWL receiver (700–4000 MHz); analysis of GP spectral structure, durations, luminosities, periodicity, wait-time distributions, energy distributions, and DM variability; sub-band search for narrow-band GPs; direct comparison with reported FRB 20200120E burst properties.
AI.result: M28A GPs show broad-band spectra (700–4000 MHz) with complex spectral peaks; no genuinely narrow-band GPs found, but narrow spectral peaks (~100 MHz) occur. Compared to FRB 20200120E, M28A GPs are 50× shorter, 10⁵× less luminous, show clear periodicity vs. none, Poissonian vs. quasi-Poissonian wait-times, and broad-band vs. only narrow-band bursts. Both have steep energy distributions and minor DM variability.
AI.conclusion: No strong links between M28A GPs and FRB 20200120E are found; the MSP-GP model for FRB 20200120E is not supported by Galactic analogues. However, an exotic MSP origin cannot be ruled out entirely, and extremely long monitoring of M28A might reveal rare ultra-luminous pulses.

title: Euclid: Early Release Observations -- The formation of peanutty dwarf galaxies in Perseus
comment: 21 pages, 18 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to A&A
summary: Dwarf galaxies in dense cluster environments are susceptible to tidal interactions that can alter their morphology and kinematics. Boxy isophotes are well studied in massive galaxies but remain poorly understood in dwarfs. We aim to identify and characterise boxy/peanutty dwarf galaxies in the Perseus cluster and determine the origin of their isophotal shapes. Using Euclid Early Release Observations of the Perseus cluster, we present a cumulative light fraction method for robustly measuring the isophotal shape parameter $c_4$, particularly suited to low surface brightness regimes. From ~1100 cataloged dwarfs, we select a clean sample of ~190 early-type systems with reliable $c_4$ measurement. Observed trends are interpreted through comparison with mock Euclid observations of $N$-body simulations of tidally transformed dwarfs. title: The giant pulse population of PSR B0355+54
comment: Submitted to Nature Astronomy
summary: Giant pulses are rare bright radio bursts that occur in restricted ranges of pulsar rotational phase. Here we report giant pulses from PSR B0355+54, a pulsar with spin period ~0.156 s. The giant pulses recur in two compact longitude regions inside the radio emission window. They are narrow compared with the mean profile, with median W50=290.3 us, and reach relative peak flux density ratios up to 149.7. The early longitude group has a timing scatter of 139.7 us, or 8.9*10^{-4} of a rotation. The first longitude group favours right, while the second favours left circular polarization.
